title: Companion, not doctor
summary: Where the companion's job ends and the doctor's begins. Read and report, never advise.

lessons.title: The golden rule
lessons.body:
> **“Main companion hoon, doctor nahi.”** (I'm a companion, not a doctor.)

Elders will ask you medical questions: “Beta, yeh goli band kar doon?” “Kya lagta hai, sugar kyon badh gaya?” Even if you study nursing or know the answer, **you never advise.** A wrong word from you can harm their health, and it breaks the family's trust.

**What you say instead:** “Uncle, yeh doctor sahab se poochna sahi rahega. Main aapke liye note kar leta hoon, agli baar pooch lenge.” Then write it down for the next visit or tell the child.

lessons.title: What you can and can't do
lessons.body:
| You CAN | You can NEVER |
| --- | --- |
| Read a prescription and explain what the doctor wrote | Suggest, change, stop or add a medicine |
| Remind them of the timing the doctor gave | Give your own opinion on a diagnosis |
| Write a medicine chart from the prescription | Give any medicine on your own, even a common one |
| Note symptoms and tell the doctor or child | Interpret a report (“sab normal hai”) |
| Read a BP or sugar machine and report the number | Say whether the number is good or bad |

If you're unsure, the answer is always: note it and ask the doctor, or tell the child.

lessons.title: Noticing without diagnosing
lessons.body:
You see the elder often. You may notice changes the family can't: more forgetfulness, low mood, weight loss, unsteady walking.

- **Do:** note it plainly in the report. “Aaj aunty ne ek hi baat 4 baar poochi, pichhle visit se zyada.”
- **Don't:** label it. Never say “lagta hai dementia hai” or “depression hai” to the elder or the family.

Your job is to observe and report. Diagnosis is the doctor's job.

questions.text: Uncle asks: “Beta, BP ki goli aaj skip kar doon? Chakkar aa raha hai.” What do you do?
options: Don't advise; tell him to check with the doctor and inform the child
questions.explanation: Never advise on medicine. Note the symptom, involve the doctor and tell the child.

questions.text: You read uncle's blood test report and it looks normal to you. What do you say?
options: Nothing about the meaning; the doctor will explain it
questions.explanation: Never interpret reports. That's the doctor's job.

questions.text: Aunty has a headache and asks you for a paracetamol from her own medicine box. What's right?
options: Don't give it yourself; ask the child or doctor what to do
questions.explanation: Never give any medicine on your own, even a common one.

questions.text: Over three visits, aunty seems more forgetful. What do you do?
options: Tell her she may have dementia
Note the change plainly in the report
questions.explanation: Observe and report plainly. Never label or diagnose.

questions.text: Which of these CAN a companion do?
options: Explain what the doctor wrote on the prescription
Stop a medicine that causes side effects
Tell the family the diagnosis is not serious
questions.explanation: Read and explain only. Never change anything.

questions.text: The BP machine shows 160/100. What do you do?
options: Report the exact number to the child or doctor without interpreting it
questions.explanation: Read and report numbers. Never say whether they're good or bad.

questions.text: You're a nursing student and know a lot about medicines. Does the golden rule apply to you?
questions.explanation: On a PeakAge visit, you are a companion. The rule applies to everyone.
